Applicant suggests that seepage from the upper reservoir could be as great as 5 cfs and could provide a source of high quality water at groundwater temperatures. As the average flow of Bad Creek and West Bad Creek combined is about 5.5 cfs, seepage would at best approximate the combined average flow from these two tributaries. During times when natural flows were above the average, seepage would appear to not compensate for the lost flow of Bad and West Bad Creeks.
Although a flow augmentation system would be placed in the upper reservoir during project construction, its use would depend on the quality of water available during project operation, particularly with regard to temperature. With the proposed construction of a submerged weir in the Whitewater arm of Lake Jocassee, the water pumped into the upper reservoir could be above the upper temperature limit of optimum trout habitat of 21°C during the summer months and unacceptable for flow augmentation purposes. During the period of June through September, augmentation would at best be at a flow rate of less than that in Howard Creek at the same time. In its letter of comment on the application for license, dated July 2, 1974, the SCWMRD stated that: "There does not appear to be a supplemental water source of sufficient quality and suitable temperatures in the area to augment flows in Howard Creek replacing those lost through the impoundment of the two small tributaries. Augmentation from a tap through the dam has questionable practicality due to elevated temperatures and initially high turbidity." In addition to determining the feasibility of flow augmentation from a quality standpoint, the volume of flow necessary to maintain and enhance the existing trout fishery and fish food organisms in Howard Creek should also be determined. The results of studies of flow augmentation and dam seepage should be made available to appropriate State and Federal agencies for comments and recommendations relative to water quality and the existing trout fishery in Howard Creek.
